item.title: Bridge change-of-measure for propagator estimation of diffusions
item.description: arXiv:2610.30213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The propagator of one-dimensional diffusions has relevant applications in statistical inference and across many disciplines. Yet it is obtained in closed form only for very few simple models. Here we analyze an importance sampling strategy based on a bridge change of measure to estimate propagators: paths are generated under an auxiliary diffusion whose bridge between the two fixed boundary points is easy to generate, and the target propagator is recovered through a Radon-Nikodym derivative or likelihood ratio correction derived from Girsanov's theorem. This method overcomes the main limitations of the crude Monte Carlo estimator, which relies on binning in state space, introducing bias and becoming inefficient with rare transitions. We apply the method to a range of benchmark processes and show that the bridge-based estimator matches the accuracy of crude Monte Carlo with orders of magnitude fewer sample paths. Finally, we elaborate on discretization schemes for the Radon-Nikodym derivative and on approximations to the best-in-class change of measure, both of which increase the efficiency of the method.
item.dc:creator: Javier Aguilar, Riccardo Gatto

item.title: Tag loss models for capture-recapture data without double tagging
item.description: arXiv:2610.30447v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard capture-recapture (CR) models assume that marked individuals do not lose their tags during the sampling period. When this assumption is violated, the estimates of model parameters can be biased. Existing tag-loss models generally rely on double-tagging all or a subset of captured individuals, permanent marks, or auxiliary information on tag retention. However, double-tagging and permanent marking may be impractical, and reliable auxiliary information may be unavailable or difficult to obtain in many situations. In this paper, we develop a novel latent multinomial modelling framework for analysis of CR data with tag loss, without requiring double-tagging or permanent marking. The proposed model framework applies to both closed-population and open-population Cormack-Jolly-Seber (CJS) settings. Through simulation studies, we demonstrate that key model parameters can be reliably estimated in both settings. We illustrate the application of the method using a dataset from a long-term study on elephant seals. The results suggest that robust inference on tag loss and demographic parameters can be achieved without double tagging, thereby avoiding logistical challenges and broadening the framework's applicability to a wider range of studies.
item.dc:creator: Katarina Skopalova, Wei Zhang

item.title: A Bayesian Copula Dirichlet Process GLM for Longitudinal Data
item.description: arXiv:2610.30467v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a semiparametric Bayesian generalized linear model (GLM) for longitudinal continuous outcomes that preserves the usual interpretation of the GLM regression structure while leaving the baseline distribution nonparametric. The proposed copula Dirichlet process generalized linear model (CDPGLM) combines a Dirichlet process prior for the baseline distribution, a parametric GLM regression structure for covariate effects, and a copula for longitudinal within--subject dependence. This construction separates modeling the marginal distribution of an individual repeated measurement from modeling the association: the Dirichlet process GLM component defines the marginal density and regression mean, whereas the copula captures dependence among repeated measurements. Compared with a parametric beta mixed--effects model, the CDPGLM provides similarly efficient estimation of regression effects while being substantially more robust to estimate marginal distributions and lower-tail probabilities (the complement of exceedance probability). In an application to data from the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) Lung Health Study, the CDPGLM and a parametric mixed beta model gave comparable inference on regression coefficients, but the CDPGLM more closely matched the empirical marginal distribution and reported more realistic and detailed lower--tail risk summaries.
item.dc:creator: Shijie Yuan, Entejar Alam, Asmit Chakraborty, Paul Rathouz, Jonathan Schildcrout, Peter M\"uller

item.title: Rematching Estimators for Average Treatment Effects
item.description: arXiv:2610.30560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Matching estimators are widely applied in practice for their great intuitive appeal. However, simple matching estimators with a fixed number of matches ($M_0$) are generally inefficient. In this article, we propose matching estimators with a variable number of matches to gain efficiency via rematching. Rather than increasing $M_0$ to gain precision, which introduces an increase in bias, the key is to rematch the treated units from the opposite direction to utilize unmatched control units. Our rematching estimators are applicable to both the average treatment effect and its counterpart for the treated population. The proposed rematching estimators are proven asymptotically valid and uniformly more efficient than matching estimators with the same $M_0$. Simulation results confirm that the proposed rematching estimators substantially improve the simple matching estimators in finite samples. As an empirical illustration, we apply the estimators proposed in this article to the National Supported Work data.
item.dc:creator: Lam Lam Hui, Kin Wai Chan

item.title: Lifetime-valid decisions by continually evolving AI analysts
item.description: arXiv:2610.30562v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents increasingly act as analysts whose decision can often be cast as hypothesis tests. Classical tests control the Type I error rate, the probability of rejecting a true null hypothesis, for fixed procedures. However, AI analysts introduce internal randomness and can evolve continuously over time. As AI analysts evolve, the risk of approving versions with Type I error rates above the target can accumulate, and adaptive use of evaluation feedback can lead to overfitting. We introduce continual validation, which evaluates each proposed AI analyst version before deployment using simulated data under the null hypothesis, with scenarios that can be randomized and expanded over time. We prove that, regardless of how updates are chosen or how many are proposed, the lifetime probability of ever deploying a version whose Type I error rate exceeds the allowed level remains bounded. This guarantees that every subsequent decision controls the Type I error rate at the target level across these scenarios. At the same time, updates with sufficiently low Type I error rates pass validation with high probability, allowing the analyst to continuously improve its performance without sacrificing rigor. In two examples involving evolving AI analysts for bioequivalence studies and product A/B tests, Type I error rates reached 0.098 and 0.183 without continual validation, compared with at most 0.045 and 0.044 with it, while retaining 82% and 96% of the power from optimally selected valid updates.
item.dc:creator: Xiaojing Sun, Yuhan Zeng, Xiao Wang

item.title: Robust M-Estimation for Spliced Power-Law Models Under Cusp-Type Non-Regularity
item.description: arXiv:2610.30624v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Statistical modeling of heavy-tailed data with bounded or finite body behaviour often relies on composite or spliced distributions characterized by structural thresholds. Because the probability density function features a sharp directional shift (a cusp) at the join point, the classical log-likelihood function exhibits a discontinuity in its first derivative, causing standard Cram\'er-Rao regularity conditions and maximum likelihood frameworks to break down. To overcome this non-regularity, we develop a robust, log-transformed asymmetric Huber M-estimation framework for the structural threshold, coupled with conditional shape maximum likelihood estimators. We derive a closed-form parameter-balancing condition that analytically guarantees Fisher consistency under structural tail asymmetry. Furthermore, we establish the joint asymptotic normality of the hybrid Maximum Likelihood and M-estimator system and derive its explicit sandwich covariance structure. A computationally efficient profiled Z-estimation algorithm is implemented to reduce the joint estimation to a one-dimensional root-finding problem. Finite-sample properties are validated through Monte Carlo simulations, and the practical utility of the framework is demonstrated on the benchmark Danish Fire Insurance claims dataset.
item.dc:creator: N Balakrishna

item.title: Behavioral Mapping of Hierarchical Dynamical Models Accelerates Bayesian Parameter Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.30683v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bayesian parameter inference for complex nonlinear dynamical models is often limited by the cost of repeated model simulation. We present a behavioral mapping framework that uses the inferred posterior of a higher-level model to accelerate inference of a lower-level model without requiring state or parameter correspondence between them. Building on approximate simulation relations for hierarchically related models, we define the notion of behavioral compatibility and quantify the behavioral support of detailed model parameters using the reduced model posterior. We learn a level set of behavioral support using a Gaussian process and use it to filter detailed model parameter proposals before expensive simulations during Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) inference. We derive conditions under which the behavioral support level set retains all detailed model parameters that fit the experimental data within a prescribed tolerance. We apply this method to a hierarchy of gene-expression models fitted to cell-free experimental data. After initial setup costs, our approach speeds up MCMC by 8.02% for the phenomenological model and 15.21% for the mechanistic model.
item.dc:creator: Jingsong Bai, Ayush Pandey

item.title: Estimating Group Average Treatment Effects in High-Risk Populations with Unobserved Target Membership
item.description: arXiv:2610.30709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Estimating treatment effects within a prespecified high-risk population is challenging. When risk status is unobserved or the target population is small, analyses restricted to high-risk individuals can be unstable or inefficient. We propose a risk-score-weighted soft-targeting (RSW) estimator for group average treatment effects in high-risk populations. It accommodates two settings: when high-risk status is observed, the membership probability can be estimated within the analysis sample; when unobserved, it can be obtained from a reference model using covariates in the analysis sample. RSW uses these probabilities to represent the target population, learns a doubly robust treatment effect in the full sample, and aggregates a low-dimensional treatment-effect surface over the risk-weighted target distribution. We establish pointwise asymptotic normality and an influence-function-based variance estimator. In simulations with continuous and binary outcomes, RSW had similar bias and lower variance than two hard-targeting alternatives. Sensitivity analyses showed that the gain persisted when treatment-effect sufficiency was violated, although RSW bias increased under strong violations. We applied the method to the All of Us study to estimate effects of non-GLP antidiabetic and antihypertensive medication use on mild cognitive impairment (MCI)-free time restricted at 48 months within comorbidity-defined high-risk subgroups. We estimated the risk score in a nonoverlapping internal reference sample and applied it to the outcome-analysis sample. This illustrates how soft targeting can improve precision while retaining an interpretable high-risk target population.
item.dc:creator: Shubo Zhang, Yinjun Zhao, Donglin Zeng, Yuanjia Wang

item.title: Beyond Global Importance: A Heterogeneity Index for Sensitivity Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.31008v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Global sensitivity analysis quantifies how strongly inputs influence a model output, however, input importance often varies across the model space. We introduce a heterogeneity index H to quantify this variation. The index compares normalized regional sensitivity profiles using mean pairwise total-variation distance and its values range from zero to one. We test H on nine benchmark functions and examine its robustness to the number of regions, sample size, and sampling strategy. We further demonstrate it using models of wooden-pallet carbon footprint, flood risk, and steel-structure reliability. Across these cases, H reveals changes in sensitivity that global indices obscure, including inputs whose importance changes substantially across the model space and differences between rare behavioral regimes. The index complements global sensitivity analysis by indicating when a single global sensitivity profile is insufficient. An open-source implementation is provided in the simdec package.
item.dc:creator: Mariia Kozlovaa, Justus Helo, Pamphile T. Roy, Julian Scott Yeomans, Andrea Saltelli

item.title: Bayes Factor Testing of Linear and Nonlinear Effects in Additive Gaussian Process Regression
item.description: arXiv:2610.31025v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Gaussian process regression flexibly models nonlinear relationships between predictors and an outcome variable. A central question in this modeling framework is whether each predictor affects the outcome linearly, nonlinearly, or not at all. We propose a Bayesian testing framework for this problem within additive Gaussian process regression. Each predictor is decomposed into a standardized linear component with a $g$-prior and an orthogonalized Gaussian process component capturing nonlinear structure. The latter is governed by a standardized magnitude parameter whose value zero removes the component. Local and non-local priors are considered for the standardized magnitude parameter. Bayes factors for testing the linear and nonlinear effects are computed from the fitted full model via Savage-Dickey-type identities, avoiding expensive marginal likelihood computations of many different models. To assess the accuracy of the Bayes factor estimates, the outcomes are compared to bridge sampling estimates. Simulations and empirical applications show the performance and applicability of the methodology.
item.dc:creator: Yueheng Wu, Joran Jongerling, Joris Mulder

item.title: On the Calibration of Isotonic Distributional Regression
item.description: arXiv:2610.31258v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Isotonic distributional regression (IDR) has recently been proposed as a non-parametric technique for probabilistic forecasting via the estimation of conditional distributions under order restrictions, based on continuous outcomes from deterministic model outputs. IDR has been widely used and multiple studies report promising performance and well-calibrated forecasts across application domains. We document a peculiar out-of-sample artifact of IDR, where probability integral transform (PIT) values are rational fractions with empirical frequencies resembling Thomae's function, an effect which thus far seems to have been overlooked. This phenomenon is demonstrated empirically using meteorological data and a simulation study. We further provide a theoretical explanation linking the spiking behavior to the discrete structure of the isotonic fits, and discuss how this artifact can be mitigated via smoothing approaches.
item.dc:creator: Tobias Biegert, Johannes Resin, Alexander Jordan, Sebastian Lerch

item.title: Generalized Infinite Hidden Markov Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.31337v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a flexible Bayesian nonparametric hidden Markov model for longitudinal data based on the hidden hierarchical Dirichlet process. Unlike the classical infinite hidden Markov model, the proposed model allows transition probabilities to change over time. In particular, this model provides a framework that operates between homogeneous and heterogeneous Markov model formulations, allowing the rows of the transition probability matrix to be clustered ac- cording to their temporal evolution. Inference is performed through a Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm, which enables the joint estimation of model parameters, latent variables, and number of states, within a unified framework. Simulation studies under both homogeneous and heterogeneous transition regimes show that the proposed model tends to recover the true latent structure, whereas the infinite hidden Markov model tends to overestimate the number of states when transitions vary over time. Two applications illustrate the ability of the model to detect changes in the transition dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe Mignemi, Daniele Tancini, Francesco Bartolucci

item.title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation and Likelihood Ratio Tests for the Power Spherical Distribution
item.description: arXiv:2610.31503v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Power Spherical distribution has been proposed as a computationally efficient alternative to the von Mises-Fisher distribution for data on the unit sphere, with reduced computational cost for simulation and a simpler normalizing constant. Despite these advantages, its statistical inference properties remain underdeveloped. In this paper, we develop a likelihood-based framework for estimation and inference for the Power Spherical distribution. Within this framework, we develop maximum likelihood estimation procedures for both the central direction and concentration parameter. Building on these estimators, we formulate likelihood ratio tests for hypotheses involving known and unknown parameters, study their asymptotic behavior, and evaluate finite-sample performance through simulation studies. The results demonstrate accurate Type I error control and good power when the asymptotic chi-square approximation is appropriate, while the parametric bootstrap provides reliable inference in small-sample settings or those where the dimension is large relative to the sample size. The findings also highlight nontrivial dependence of the power of tests for the central direction on the concentration parameter.
item.dc:creator: Sharindi Amasha Samaraweera, Leif Ellingson

item.title: More efficient transportation of causal effects using mediators
item.description: arXiv:2610.31568v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop flexible semiparametric estimators of the average treatment effect transported to a target population that leverage mediators to achieve identification, and prior knowledge of population heterogeneity or summary-level statistics to achieve improved efficiency. We first propose a one-step semiparametric estimator that assumes knowledge of the baseline covariates driving the heterogeneity across populations. This approach improves efficiency by transporting only through these covariates, rather than through the full covariate set. We then introduce a collaborative one-step semiparametric estimator that also improves efficiency without requiring knowledge of which covariates drive study heterogeneity. Collectively, these estimators advance our ability to transport causal effects by improving efficiency in the presence of mediation and intermediate confounding through targeted dimension reduction strategies. We use simulation to examine finite-sample performance and apply our estimators to a large-scale housing mobility trial (MTO) and a hearing intervention trial (ACHIEVE).
item.dc:creator: Xinyi Zhang, Kara E. Rudolph, James Russell Pike, Richard Liu, Michele Santacatterina, Iv\'an D\'iaz

item.title: A Subjective Bayesian Approach to Address Unchecked Assumptions in a Causal Analysis
item.description: arXiv:2610.31587v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Causal analyses using observational data rely on identifying assumptions that cannot be verified from the observed data alone. When such unchecked assumptions fail, effect estimates may be biased and uncertainty may be understated. We propose the Adjusted Model for Unchecked Assumptions (AMUA), a subjective Bayesian framework that propagates uncertainty about the joint validity of key causal assumptions through a two-component posterior mixture. One component corresponds to the standard observational causal model in which the assumptions hold (referred to as the "assumption-hold component"); the other represents a flexibly defined model that allows the causal assumptions to fail (referred to as the "assumption-fail component"). The mixture weight $\pi$ is specified by the analyst as the prior probability assigned to the assumption-hold component. This formulation leads to a new diagnostic, $\pi_{\min}$: the smallest value of $\pi$ for which the 95\% HPD set for the average treatment effect (ATE) excludes zero. In simulations with a spatially structured unmeasured confounder, we evaluate bias, interval length, and coverage as $\pi$ varies. The results show that acknowledging assumption uncertainty can widen intervals, and improve coverage relative to analyses that treat the assumptions as certain. In a county-level application relating long-term PM$_{2.5}$ exposure to COVID-19 mortality, AMUA shows how posterior conclusions depend on prior confidence in the identifying assumptions.
item.dc:creator: Jaiyool Kim, Indrabati Bhattacharya, Jonathan R. Bradley

item.title: Volatility-Corrected Prediction Intervals: Locally Adaptive Uncertainty Quantification for Probabilistic Time-Series Forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2610.31621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Prediction intervals from probabilistic time-series forecasters are commonly assessed by marginal coverage, the long-run proportion of observations falling inside the intervals. However, forecast errors in time series are often serially dependent and heteroskedastic, so prediction intervals can attain near-nominal marginal coverage while miscovering systematically during periods of larger local error variance. We identify and address this failure mode, which we call \emph{local scale miscalibration}. We first document the phenomenon using time-series foundation models (TSFMs): across several real-world series, their native intervals often attain near-nominal marginal coverage while exhibiting substantial temporal variation in local coverage, alternating between overcoverage and undercoverage over shorter windows. We then propose Volatility-Corrected Prediction Intervals (VCPI), a post-hoc calibration procedure that uses the base forecaster's predictive scale as a baseline, models the volatility of standardized forecast residuals with a Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) model, and applies a multiplicative correction to produce locally adaptive prediction intervals. We justify VCPI both theoretically and empirically, comparing it against model-agnostic conformal counterparts. We provide a theoretical analysis of interval adaptation of the proposed method following abrupt changes in volatility. Empirically, we evaluate VCPI on Chronos, Moirai, and TimesFM across four real-world datasets and find that it produces more stable local coverage than conformal baselines while maintaining near-nominal marginal coverage and comparable interval width.
item.dc:creator: Jason B. Cho, David S. Matteson

item.title: Elimination Geometry II: Integrability, Representation, and Structural Limits
item.description: arXiv:2610.30145v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Elimination geometry studies the exact nonnegative defect left after an auxiliary variable is optimized out. Part~II audits this certified-elimination interface through three theorem families. For integrability, local gaps form a repeated partial-elimination tower precisely under nonnegativity, touching, and zero elementary-square circulation. Hodge projection constructs nearest finite-space repairs and separates curvature, certification, and global period taxes. For representation and price, a descent gate characterizes surjective refinements and rules out strictly convex separable, duplication-invariant weight penalties. Dummy and target-calling lifts show that unrestricted lift design is vacuous, whereas the Fidelity-coherence frontier isolates irreducible cost. A modal Gram block classifies unconstrained quadratic lift-coupling germs and yields aligned Gaussian risk ledgers. Bernstein spectral functions preserve graph-Laplacian structure. Graph-universal Markov resolvents exist exactly up to first-order fractional qualification, and universal polynomial spectral penalties reduce to nonnegative Laplacian multiples. This linear limit does not preclude Part~I's nonlinear CDF repair and sharp CRPS theory. For converses, finite-order target-jet preservation uniquely requires subtraction of the corresponding defect jet, up to flat terms; approximate jets yield quasi-descent and stationary limits. Fixed-marginal coupling obeys a dependence-benefit frontier. Reversing certified KL in entropy-regularized control eliminates dimension-free guarantees, while a fixed measurement preserves all Umegaki defects of a faithful Gibbs family exactly when that family commutes.
item.dc:creator: Mian Huang, Xueqin Wang

item.title: Triple Products of Correlated Multivariate Hermite Polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2610.30204v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stochastic Galerkin schemes (SGS) are used to approximate solutions to differential equations with stochastic parameters. In particular, they express the solution with an infinite orthogonal functional basis of the parameter space and derive a deterministic system of PDEs; the solution of this deterministic system can be used to produce a {surrogate} approximation of the original stochastic equations. When the parameters are correlated, the infinite series representation of the solution does not provably converge for all joint distributions; further, classic decorrelating transformations (e.g., Roseblatt) often introduce known numerical instabilities. Rahman (2017) established convergence in probability and distribution for correlated {Gaussian} parameters when the basis functionals are {multivariate Hermite polynomials} (MHPs), where these polynomials are only {weakly orthogonal} with respect to the underlying joint density. Due to weak orthogonality, the $N$th moments of MHPs introduced during Galerkin projection do not trivially decompose into products of one-dimensional expectations and have no closed-form expression for $N > 2$; consequently, these moments are typically estimated via brute-force sampling and quickly become prohibitively expensive to compute. In this paper, we introduce and prove several foundational results for MHPs. These results culminate in an equation that can be used to calculate the $N = 3$ moments (triple products) exactly, whose implementation dramatically reduces the computational bottleneck otherwise inherent to SGS with correlated Gaussian parameters.
item.dc:creator: Laura Lyman

item.title: When Reconstruction Is Not Enough: Doubly Robust Counterfactual and Interventional Mediation Analysis with Learned Multimodal Representations
item.description: arXiv:2610.30220v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Learned representations of high-dimensional multimodal health records are increasingly used to adjust for confounding, yet they are usually trained to reconstruct the data rather than preserve the information that causal identification requires. We study counterfactual outcomes under alternative treatments, including phenotype-specific effects and patient-level counterfactual risk profiles of the kind digital twins provide, and interventional direct and indirect effects under exposure-induced intermediate confounding. We give conditions under which a representation preserves identification and show that interventional mediation is more demanding than counterfactual comparison. We prove that no covariate-only training objective, whether reconstruction, contrastive, or physics-informed, can certify that a representation is sufficient, and that, in a linear structural model, a representation can lose arbitrarily little reconstruction accuracy yet induce arbitrarily large bias. We decompose the error of cross-fitted doubly robust estimators into a first-order representation bias, which neither double robustness nor cross-fitting removes, and a second-order remainder of nuisance-estimation errors, so coverage worsens as the sample size grows when the representation is insufficient. We propose a workflow combining modality-specific variational autoencoders trained outside the estimation sample, cross-fitted doubly robust estimators, locked phenotypes, select-then-confirm pathway analysis, portable representations, and diagnostics for representation insufficiency, exposure leakage, and sensitivity. In simulations, discarding a rare, moderately strong confounder gave indirect-effect intervals with 2% coverage at n = 3,000; reconstruction loss missed the problem, and a simple predictive diagnostic flagged it in every replicate.
item.dc:creator: Cong Cao

item.title: Prediction Uncertainty Controlled Computer Model Calibration
item.description: arXiv:2610.31163v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Computer-model calibration is usually undertaken in service of prediction, yet neither Bayesian Kennedy-O'Hagan (KOH) calibration nor amortized simulation-based inference is built to control the predictive error of the calibrated simulator. When parameters are weakly identified or the data-model discrepancy is misspecified, the simulator-output bands induced by a nominal posterior level can be far from nominal. We propose a two-layer framework that targets predictive miscoverage directly. First, a conditional flow-matching model learns an amortized posterior for the calibration parameters, trained on simulator outputs perturbed with Gaussian-process discrepancies of varying structure. Second, conformal risk control arranges posterior draws for the target observation into nested candidate sets and selects the smallest one whose fixed-rank pointwise bands attain a prescribed time-averaged miscoverage on a synthetic calibration sample. Under exchangeability of calibration and target observations, the bands control expected miscoverage in finite samples. In a synthetic benchmark, the proposed bands are roughly 20% the width of KOH-MCMC bands with miscoverage near the 10% target. In calibrating an age-structured SEIR model to the 2010 Malawi measles outbreak, they are again sharper and near-nominal, and the weeks they fail to cover coincide with the asymmetric epidemic decline, exposing structural inadequacy of the mechanistic model.
item.dc:creator: Ryan Heejoon Byun, Dayeon Yoon, Won Chang

item.title: Deep Learning for Random Objects in Metric Spaces: Beyond Manifold Assumptions
item.description: arXiv:2610.31328v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Deep learning (DL) methods have substantially improved predictive performance across a wide range of downstream prediction tasks, enabling new discoveries in multiple domains. However, principled DL methods for non-Euclidean random objects remain relatively scarce, despite the growing importance of modern biomedical outcomes taking the form of probability distributions, random graphs, functions, and other random objects in metric spaces. Motivated by a new generation of digital and clinical biomarkers, we propose a deep learning framework for regression with random objects in metric spaces. Our approach operates directly on the metric structure of the response space, avoiding restrictive manifold or Euclidean embedding assumptions imposed by many existing methods. At the same time, it retains modern statistical guarantees under the stated statistical assumptions. We establish statistical consistency and convergence rates for the proposed estimator, and characterize conditions under which it can mitigate the curse of dimensionality for hierarchically compositional regression functions. Extensive simulation studies demonstrate competitive predictive performance, with gains over several competing approaches in multiple Euclidean and non-Euclidean configurations. Finally, we demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed framework in two digital health case studies with distribution-valued outcomes in Wasserstein spaces, using high-resolution accelerometry and continuous glucose monitoring data. Embedding-based deep-learning methods may be less suitable when no informative low-dimensional representation exists or when the learned embedding does not adequately preserve the intrinsic geometry of the response space.
item.dc:creator: Marcos Matabuena, Xiaokai Luo, Oscar Hernan Madrid Padilla

item.title: Reliable AI-Assisted Decisions via Selective Auditing
item.description: arXiv:2610.31662v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We consider online monitoring of an AI system that produces a sequence of decisions. At each round, the system outputs a proposed decision together with a confidence score estimating the trustworthiness of the decision. The decision and confidence score need not be produced by the same model: for example, one agent may propose a decision, while a separate verifier agent evaluates it and outputs a correctness or safety score. Based on this information, we must decide whether to accept the AI decision automatically or consult an expert, such as a human auditor, who reviews the proposal and either accepts or corrects it. We formulate this task as an online constrained optimization problem in which the goal is to minimize the frequency of expert auditing while guaranteeing that the fraction of AI errors that go unaudited stays below a user-defined threshold. We derive a family of algorithms with provable error-control guarantees with no assumptions, including a method that is optimally efficient: it asymptotically attains the best achievable auditing rate for both adversarial and i.i.d. data streams. Experiments on screening harmful requests to large language models, qualitative text annotation, and data labeling show that our methods achieve valid error control in practice while substantially reducing the need for human auditing compared to baselines.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Gibbs, Elise L. Han, Ryan J. Tibshirani, Tijana Zrnic

item.title: Automatic Differentiation for Inference on Partially Observed Markov Process Models
item.description: arXiv:2407.03085v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Automatic differentiation (AD) has driven recent advances in machine learning, including deep neural networks and Hamiltonian Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Partially observed nonlinear stochastic dynamical systems have proved resistant to AD techniques because widely used particle filter algorithms yield an estimated likelihood function that is discontinuous as a function of the model parameters. To resolve this, we create a theoretical framework that embeds two existing AD particle filter methods within a new class of algorithms. This new class permits a bias-variance tradeoff and hence a mean squared error substantially lower than the existing algorithms. This allows us to develop likelihood maximization algorithms suited to the Monte Carlo properties of the AD gradient estimate. Our algorithms require only a differentiable simulator for the latent dynamic system; by contrast, most previous approaches to AD likelihood maximization for particle filters require access to the system's transition probabilities. Numerical results indicate that a hybrid algorithm, using AD to refine a coarse solution from an iterated filtering algorithm, shows substantial improvement on current state-of-the-art methods on a challenging scientific benchmark problem.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Tan, Aaron J. Abkemeier, Kunyang He, Giles Hooker, Edward L. Ionides

item.title: Sharp Bounds on the Variance of General Regression Adjustment in Randomized Experiments
item.description: arXiv:2411.00191v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: A growing statistical literature focuses on causal inference in the context of experiments where the target of inference is the average treatment effect in a finite population and random assignment determines which subjects are allocated to one of the experimental conditions. In this framework, variances of average treatment effect estimators remain unidentified because they depend on the covariance between treated and untreated potential outcomes, which are never jointly observed. Conventional variance estimators are upwardly biased. Recent work provides an estimator for the variance of the difference-in-means estimator that is asymptotically sharp. The practical relevance of this result, however, remains limited, as researchers often rely on some form of covariate adjustment, such as linear regression, when estimating the average treatment effect. Adapting propositions from empirical process theory, we provide asymptotically sharp variance estimators for general regression adjustment. We apply these results to linear regression adjustment and show benefits both in a simulation and in three empirical applications drawn from different disciplines.
item.dc:creator: Jonas M. Mikhaeil, Donald P. Green

item.title: Causal Inference Under Network Interference
item.description: arXiv:2508.06808v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We review the growing body of research on the challenging topic of interference in causal inference. Interference arises when the treatment assignments of connected units affect the outcomes of other units directly (via spillover) or indirectly (via contagion). Examples include public health, economic, political, or educational interventions, as well as advertising on social media. Adapting the Neyman-Rubin potential outcome framework, we review selected causal effects under interference and discuss identification of causal effects based on experimental and observational data. We then review statistical tests for interference and causal effects, design- and model-based estimators for causal effects, and methodological challenges, including variance reduction, unknown interference graphs, and misspecified exposure mappings. We conclude with a discussion of the scope of causal conclusions based on fixed and random potential outcomes and interference graphs. While the fixed potential outcome framework is sufficient in many applications, the random potential outcome framework can be useful when the data fall short. Examples include causal inference for heterogeneous treatment effects and external validity, including generalizability and transportability.
item.dc:creator: Subhankar Bhadra, Michael Schweinberger

item.title: Can discrete-time analyses be trusted for stepped wedge trials with continuous recruitment?
item.description: arXiv:2511.18731v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In stepped wedge cluster randomized trials (SW-CRTs), the intervention is rolled out to clusters sequentially over multiple periods. It is common practice to analyze data from SW-CRTs using linear mixed models that treat time as discrete. However, a recent systematic review found that 95.1\% of cross-sectional SW-CRTs recruit individuals continuously over time. Despite the prevalence of continuous recruitment, there has been limited guidance on how to draw model-robust inference for such designs. In this article, we conduct simulation studies to examine the performance of discrete-time linear mixed models in the case of continuous recruitment designs with a continuous outcome. Specifically, we generate outcomes under a continuous-time exponential decay correlation structure with either discrete or continuous fixed period effects. We consider constant and exposure-time-dependent intervention effects, with and without random intervention effects across clusters. We then analyze the simulated data using linear mixed models under three discrete-time working correlation structures: simple exchangeable, nested exchangeable, and discrete-time exponential decay, with robust sandwich variance estimation. Our results demonstrate that discrete-time analysis often yields negligible bias and that the robust variance estimator with the Mancl and DeRouen correction consistently achieves nominal coverage and type I error rate. However, when recruitment patterns vary systematically between control and intervention periods, discrete-time analyses give slightly biased intervention effect estimates. Finally, we illustrate these findings by reanalyzing a completed SW-CRT.
item.dc:creator: Hao Wang, Guangyu Tong, Heather Allore, Kelsey L. Grantham, Monica Taljaard, Fan Li

item.title: Penalized Fair Regression for Multiple Groups in Chronic Kidney Disease
item.description: arXiv:2512.17340v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fair regression methods have the potential to mitigate societal bias concerns in health care, but there has been little work on penalized fair regression when multiple groups experience such bias. We propose a general regression framework that addresses this gap with unfairness penalties for multiple groups. Our approach is demonstrated for binary outcomes with true positive rate disparity penalties. It can be efficiently implemented through reduction to a cost-sensitive classification problem. We additionally introduce novel score functions for automatically selecting penalty weights. Our penalized fair regression methods are empirically studied in simulations, where they achieve a fairness-accuracy frontier beyond that of existing comparison methods. Finally, we apply these methods to a national multi-site primary care study of chronic kidney disease to develop a fair classifier for end-stage renal disease. There we find substantial improvements in fairness for multiple race and ethnicity groups who experience societal bias in the health care system without any appreciable loss in overall fit.
item.dc:creator: Carter H. Nakamoto, Lucia Lushi Chen, Agata Foryciarz, Sherri Rose

item.title: Automated selection of $r$ in $r$-largest order statistics models: finite-sample performance and return-level inference
item.description: arXiv:2602.23909v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Selecting the number $r$ of upper order statistics is a key practical issue in fitting $r$-largest order statistics models. The entropy difference test for selecting $r$ relies on a large-sample approximation. The score test can be used for small samples but is computationally demanding. To obtain a fast method that is also applicable to small samples, we propose a method based on the conditional cumulative distribution function (CCDF), which applies a sequence of Cram\'er--von Mises goodness-of-fit tests. The tests are calibrated by a parametric bootstrap in which each refit is replaced by a single Newton step, so the computation remains fast. We also revisit the spacings test and show that the two test statistics become nearly identical as $r$ increases. Monte Carlo simulations show that the CCDF test has accurate size and good power in small and moderate samples. Further simulations show that a few additional order statistics can reduce the error of return-level estimates compared with those obtained from the block maxima only. The method is illustrated using rainfall data from Sancheong, Korea.
item.dc:creator: Yire Shin, Jihong Park, Jeong-Soo Park

item.title: Robust Twoblock Simultaneous Dimension Reduction and Multivariate Regression
item.description: arXiv:2603.24820v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper introduces robust twoblock (RTB) simultaneous dimension reduction, which is the first statistically robust method to perform simultaneous dimension reduction in two blocks of variables that allows to tune the number of components in each block individually. The paper proposes both a dense and a sparse version of the new method. Sparse RTB is the first robust estimator of this kind that allows to tune both the number of components and the degree of sparsity (i.e.\ the number of variables retained) for each block individually. RTB thereby allows to optimally extract and summarize the relevant portion of information in each block of data, also in the presence of outliers. As a corollary, the estimators can be recombined into a single estimate of regression coefficients for multivariate regression that is operable when the number of variables exceeds the number of cases in each block. An extensive simulation study illustrates that the new methods are resistant to different types of outliers, while maintaining estimation efficiency across a range of dimensionality settings. These findings both hold true for the dense and the sparse method. The methods' performance is further illustrated on two example data sets and a straightforward algorithm is presented and made accessible in an open source repository.
item.dc:creator: Sven Serneels

item.title: Identification of Latent Group Effects under Conditional Calibration
item.description: arXiv:2604.08798v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study identification of a structural group effect when the group indicator $G\in\{0,1\}$ is unobserved but the analyst observes a calibrated probability score $p$ satisfying $E[G\mid p,X]=p$. Under a constant-coefficient structural mean model, the latent-group coefficient $\tau$ is point-identified by a closed-form ratio of observable moments whose denominator is the residual score variance $V^{*}=E[(p-E[p\mid X])^2]$. Identification fails exactly when the score is a deterministic function of $X$; we construct an explicit continuum of observationally equivalent models showing the failure is genuine. The marginal latent mean gap decomposes as $\tau$ plus a compositional term that is itself identified in closed form, and we characterise when the two coincide. The oracle estimator is $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and asymptotically normal with a closed-form sandwich variance. Under calibration error bounded by $\delta$, the bias obeys a sharp bound proportional to $\delta/V^{*}$, and hard-threshold classification attenuates the estimated gap. Monte Carlo experiments confirm the theory, including the variance-weighted estimand under heterogeneous effects.
item.dc:creator: Marcell T. Kurbucz

item.title: PCA score regression: the art of losing power
item.description: arXiv:2605.24118v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The regression of principal component scores (RPCS) on covariates is a widely used analytic approach to detect and test for associations between functional measurements and study participant characteristics. Here we show that: (1) RPCS loses power relative to Function on Scalar Regression (FoSR); (2) the amount of power loss depends on the correlation between the PCs and the true effect; (3) if not corrected for multiplicity, RPCS has inflated $\alpha$-level; and (4) current RPCS methods do not provide valid inference for the true effect. In contrast, we show that Function on Scalar Regression (FoSR) can avoid these problems using a particular combination of modeling tools. We validate these theoretical findings through extensive simulations and illustrate their practical implications using minute-level accelerometry data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES).
item.dc:creator: Yu Lu, Nidhi Pai, Erjia Cui, Ciprian Crainiceanu

item.title: Beyond Exchangeability: Distribution-Shift-Aware Integration of External Control Data in Randomized Trials
item.description: arXiv:2605.28785v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) are the gold standard for evaluating causal effects but are often costly and difficult to scale; consequently, they are frequently augmented with auxiliary external controls in many applications. Prior approaches to borrowing such data typically rely on exchangeability, under which the external controls are readily usable for inference in the trial population. In practice, however, differences in eligibility criteria, standard of care, and data collection procedures may induce distribution shifts between the RCT and the external controls, making exchangeability implausible. In this paper, we propose a general framework for incorporating external controls that explicitly accounts for distribution shifts through an augmented estimating function, allowing information about the shifts to be leveraged for efficiency gains even when exchangeability does not hold. To guard against potential bias and efficiency loss due to misspecification of the distribution shift, we further develop an adaptive shrinkage estimator that preserves consistency while guaranteeing efficiency dominance over the trial-only benchmark. Synthetic experiments and a real data application demonstrate the practical advantages of the proposed approaches.
item.dc:creator: Jiawei Shan, Yiteng Tu, Guanbo Wang, Chao Ying, Jiwei Zhao

item.title: Bayesian Graphical Models under Positivity Constraints: A Scalable Generalized Likelihood Approach
item.description: arXiv:2607.26469v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We develop a computationally scalable Bayesian framework for precision matrix estimation in Gaussian graphical models under total positivity constraints. To overcome the high computational cost of the Gaussian likelihood, we adopt a generalized Bayesian approach based on the D-trace loss, which eliminates the log-determinant term and enables efficient optimization while allowing relaxation of positive definiteness during sampling. Sparsity is induced via spike-and-slab priors, and the resulting generalized posterior is shown to be proper under mild conditions. Our primary contribution is a suite of efficient posterior sampling algorithms tailored to high-dimensional settings. Starting from a component-wise Gibbs sampler, we introduce a novel data augmentation scheme that induces conditional independence among precision matrix entries, enabling joint updates. By exploiting the Gram structure of the sample covariance matrix, we further develop a fast matrix-normal sampler that significantly reduces per-iteration complexity in high-dimensional settings. An interweaving strategy combines augmented and direct updates to improve mixing without sacrificing scalability. Experiments on synthetic and financial data demonstrate substantial computational gains over existing methods, while maintaining competitive estimation accuracy and improved recovery of structured dependencies.
item.dc:creator: Swarnali Raha, Partha Sarkar, Sirani M. Perera, Kshitij Khare

item.title: Two-Point Dependent Wild Bootstrap for Weakly Dependent Estimating Equations
item.description: arXiv:2609.32369v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper develops a general two-point dependent wild bootstrap (DWB) for weakly dependent estimating equations. Its key feature is that the two-point marginal distribution and the latent serial dependence specification can be chosen separately. The construction combines a normalized two-point distribution with a stationary latent Gaussian process via a Gaussian copula transformation, includes dependent Rademacher and Mammen multipliers, and nests the classical iid two-point wild bootstrap as the serially independent case. The induced multiplier autocovariances determine the lag weights in a corresponding heteroskedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent (HAC) covariance estimator, which coincides exactly with the conditional covariance of the bootstrap estimating-equation sum. We establish first-order bootstrap validity for asymptotically linear estimators by showing that the matched-HAC estimator consistently estimates the long-run covariance and that the bootstrap estimating-equation sum converges conditionally to the same Gaussian limit as its original-sample counterpart, yielding valid HAC-studentized $z$-tests and the corresponding Wald and Lagrange multiplier tests. Monte Carlo experiments in nonlinear generalized method of moments (GMM) and linear regression, with common HAC studentization and matched multiplier covariances, show that dependent Rademacher generally yields better size control than Mammen and Gaussian DWB, especially for restricted $z$-tests. An application illustrates differences between asymptotic and bootstrap inference.
item.dc:creator: Mikihito Nishi, Takashi Yamagata

item.title: Strong Simultaneous Inference for Restricted Mean Survival Time Processes in Multi-Arm Trials under Covariate-Adaptive Randomization
item.description: arXiv:2610.27466v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Confirmatory trials increasingly test several treatments against a common control, and many balance prognostic factors through covariate-adaptive randomization (CAR). For time-to-event endpoints, they usually rely on the stratified log-rank test and the hazard ratio, but the former may lose power and the latter its clear interpretation when hazards are not proportional. The restricted mean survival time (RMST) provides an interpretable alternative, yet inference for multiple RMST comparisons under CAR remains largely unexplored. We first derive the joint asymptotic distribution of the standard Kaplan--Meier RMST estimators in multi-arm trials. Under Pocock--Simon minimization, their limiting covariance contains a design term that arises only when the randomization factors interact in their effect on survival. A stratum-standardized estimator removes this term and remains valid when censoring depends on the strata. We then develop test statistics that account for the shared control and the randomization design. Calibrated by a Gaussian multiplier, the resulting max-$T$ procedures control the family-wise error rate and give simultaneous confidence bands over restriction times. In simulations, the method controls the Type I error rate under various randomization procedures and outperforms the stratified log-rank test when the benefit wanes. An application based on the three-arm ICON6 trial illustrates its practicality.
item.dc:creator: Guannan Zhai, Feifang Hu

item.title: Inference on Quantile Treatment Effects with Small Treatment Groups
item.description: arXiv:2105.10965v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop inference for conditional quantile treatment effects that allows treatment groups to remain small as the overall sample grows. Such groups arise naturally in multivalued treatment models. Our procedure combines estimation of a conditional quantile function from a large reference group with an exact conditional Bernoulli representation of quantile indicators. We establish asymptotic size control and derive a power bound allowing treatment-group sizes to remain bounded. The framework accommodates nonseparable outcome functions, heteroskedasticity, and flexible error distributions across treatment profiles. We illustrate its scope through dynamic treatment models, nonseparable quantile models, and difference-in-differences designs with staggered adoption. Monte Carlo experiments assess finite-sample performance, and an application to temperature shocks and GDP growth illustrates inference on effects associated with distinct treatment histories.
item.dc:creator: Marina Dias, Demian Pouzo

item.title: The Anatomy of Dependence in Multivariate Ordered Choice
item.description: arXiv:2205.05779v5 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: When individuals make simultaneous decisions across multiple ordered dimensions, standard multivariate ordered choice models impose narrow bracketing, with each dimension decided as if the others did not exist. We develop a general rectangular structure model capturing broad bracketing while nesting the standard model. The framework introduces two layers of dependence, one through the threshold structure associated with decision rules and the other through the correlation of latent utilities. We provide microfoundations, prove identification, and discuss estimation. We showcase the model in applications to parental investment in children's education, cryptocurrency familiarity and expectations, and health insurance, where the latter separates moral hazard from adverse selection.
item.dc:creator: Tatiana Komarova, William Matcham

item.title: Marital Sorting, Household Inequality and Selection
item.description: arXiv:2310.07839v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Using CPS data for 1976 to 2025, we explore how wage inequality has evolved for married couples with both spouses working full time full year, and its impact on household income inequality. We also investigate how marriage sorting patterns have changed over this period. To determine the factors driving income inequality we estimate a model explaining the joint distribution of couples' wages that accounts for spouses' employment decisions. This requires a multivariate distribution regression model that incorporates a double selection rule. We find that income inequality has increased for these households and increased wage sorting has exacerbated the inequality resulting from individual wage growth. We find that positive sorting partially reflects the correlation across unobservables influencing the wages of both members of the marriage. We decompose the changes in sorting patterns over the 50-year sample into structural, composition and selection effects and find that the increase in positive sorting primarily reflects the increased skill premia for both observed and unobserved characteristics.
item.dc:creator: Iv\'an Fern\'andez-Val, Aico van Vuuren, Francis Vella

item.title: Optimal Clustering of Multi-layer Networks under Mixture Block Models
item.description: arXiv:2311.15598v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study clustering for multi-layer networks, where each observation is an undirected network measured on the same set of vertices. Under the mixture multi-layer stochastic block model (MMSBM), each network is generated from one of two stochastic block models, and the goal is to recover the latent network labels. We establish the minimax optimal network clustering error rate, which takes an exponential form and is characterized by the Chernoff information between the edge probability distributions of the component networks. We propose a novel two-stage estimator that combines tensor-based initialization, node and sample splitting, and a likelihood-based refinement. The refinement step exploits estimated node communities and achieves the minimax rate with high probability under extreme network sparsity. We further extend the likelihood-refinement framework to count-weighted networks through a mixture multi-layer Poisson block model. Numerical studies and two real-data analyses illustrate the finite-sample behavior of the proposed method and its use for both external-label benchmarking and unlabeled exploratory network clustering.
item.dc:creator: Zhongyuan Lyu, Ting Li, Dong Xia

item.title: Fast Approximate Modular Inference for Option Price Prediction
item.description: arXiv:2412.00658v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: A new approximate Bayesian inferential framework is proposed that exploits multiple information sources -- daily spot returns, high-frequency spot data and option prices -- and enables fast calculation of probabilistic predictions of future option prices. This approach operates directly from the theoretical option pricing model, and does not require an explicit statistical model, or likelihood, for the observed option prices. We demonstrate that our approach achieves predictive accuracy comparable to likelihood-based modular inference, despite not explicitly modelling option-pricing errors, while delivering substantial computational gains. Predictive accuracy based on the Heston option pricing model is illustrated empirically for short-maturity options, with the rapidity of real-time updates of the predictive distributions highlighted.
item.dc:creator: Worapree Maneesoonthorn, David T. Frazier, Gael M. Martin

item.title: Sparse Equation Matching: A Derivative-Free Learning for General-Order Dynamical Systems
item.description: arXiv:2507.20072v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Equation discovery is a fundamental learning task for uncovering the underlying dynamics of complex systems, with wide-ranging applications in areas such as brain connectivity analysis, climate modeling, gene regulation, and physical simulation. However, many existing approaches rely on accurate derivative estimation and are limited to first-order dynamical systems, restricting their applicability in real-world scenarios. In this work, we propose Sparse Equation Matching (SEM), a unified framework that encompasses several existing equation discovery methods under a common formulation. SEM introduces an integral-based sparse regression approach using Green's functions, enabling derivative-free estimation of differential operators and their associated driving functions in general-order dynamical systems. The effectiveness of SEM is demonstrated through extensive simulations, benchmarking its performance against derivative-based approaches. We then apply SEM to electroencephalographic (EEG) data recorded during multiple oculomotor tasks, collected from 52 participants in a brain-computer interface experiment. Our method identifies active brain regions across participants and reveals task-specific connectivity patterns. These findings offer valuable insights into brain connectivity and the underlying neural mechanisms.
item.dc:creator: Jiaqiang Li, Jianbin Tan, Xueqin Wang

item.title: Multiply Robust Conformal Risk Control with Coarsened Data
item.description: arXiv:2508.15489v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conformal Prediction (CP) provides prediction sets with formal coverage guarantees, but most existing methods assume fully observed training and calibration data. In many applications, however, outcomes, covariates, or both may be missing or coarsened. We develop a general framework for predictive inference with coarsened data by combining semiparametric theory with conformal methods. We introduce two complementary procedures. $(i)$ Robust Split Prediction (RSP) generalizes the doubly robust estimating-equation approach of Yang et al. [2024] beyond the classical missing outcome problem by constructing an efficient influence function based estimating equation and solving its empirical analogue. This yields multiply robust prediction sets under general coarsening patterns. $(ii)$ Robust Split Conformal Prediction (RSCP) instead combines semiparametric theory with conformal risk control. Because efficient influence functions are generally non-monotone in the threshold, we first estimate the target threshold on an independent sample and freeze the threshold-dependent nuisance functions at this preliminary estimate. This restores monotonicity and allows standard conformal risk control arguments to be applied. The resulting coverage guarantees inherit the higher-order mixed-bias structure of the influence function. We develop the theory for classical, multi-stage monotone, and non-monotone missingness and illustrate the performance of the methods through simulations and a longitudinal rheumatoid-arthritis application.
item.dc:creator: Manit Paul, Arun Kumar Kuchibhotla, Eric J. Tchetgen Tchetgen

item.title: An E-value Reanalysis of DESI's Dynamical Dark Energy Signal
item.description: arXiv:2607.28918v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cosmological surveys such as DESI release data in stages, and each release reprocesses earlier observations and supersedes its predecessor. Testing the same hypothesis at every release inflates the false-positive rate, and only the collaboration can estimate the cross-release covariance that an exact combination needs. We show how to combine evidence across such releases using public products alone. From each release we compute an e-value, a non-negative statistic with expectation at most one under the null, and we average these e-values with weights fixed in advance. Provided each release's own likelihood is correct, this average controls the false-positive rate at every release under arbitrary dependence between releases. For DESI BAO at a fixed Planck background, DR2 alone gives an e-value of $33.97$ against $\Lambda$CDM ($p \le 0.0295$) under our reference test specification, a flat prior on $(w_0, w_a)$ over a fixed box. The equal-weight average of DR1 and DR2 is $17.51$ ($p \le 0.0571$), below the rejection threshold of $20$. We did not fix these weights before DR2 was published, and the weights we now fix ahead of DR3 give $p \le 0.0874$ at DR2. Without a model of the cross-release covariance, an exact combination that counts each observation once can take any value. Under explicit models it ranges from below the threshold to nearly double the DR2 value, depending on the structure assumed. The evidence is concentrated in the LRG2 bin, which also changed most between releases. Without it the DR2 e-value falls to $0.49$, and a look-elsewhere correction over the seven redshift bins leaves no rejection. DR2 does not reject under wider priors either. The signal is therefore fragile and specification-dependent. We recommend that surveys report per-release e-values with a stated test specification and a combination rule fixed in advance, and publish the cross-release covariance.
item.dc:creator: Jinyoung Kim (Stanford University, Two Sigma Investments), David F. Mota (University of Oslo), Andrius Tamosiunas (University of Oslo, Case Western Reserve University)

item.title: When Prediction Error Is Not Enough: Evaluating Nuisance-Function Prediction for Causal Estimation
item.description: arXiv:2609.00071v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Prediction error is widely used to evaluate nuisance-function estimators in causal inference, but its relationship with the performance of the resulting causal estimator is not well understood. We studied this question in a partially linear model using Monte Carlo simulations, comparing ordinary least squares (OLS), generalized additive models (GAMs), XGBoost, and Double Machine Learning with XGBoost (DML-XGBoost) with independent and with clustered observations. We evaluated nuisance-function prediction error, bias, RMSE, and 95% confidence interval coverage, and derived the second-order remainder through which errors in the exposure and outcome nuisance functions jointly determine the bias of the residualized estimator. When all methods estimated the causal effect from the same training sample, DML-XGBoost had the lowest RMSE and the highest coverage among the non-oracle methods, although XGBoost fitted to the full training sample had lower out-of-sample prediction error for both nuisance functions. GAMs had the lowest prediction error of all methods but were biased, with coverage of 0.55 with independent observations. The remainder reproduced the average bias of OLS, GAMs, and DML-XGBoost, but only half to three-quarters of the bias of XGBoost, whose residuals were formed on the data used to fit it. A joint-error measure based on the absolute cross-product of the two nuisance errors was only weakly associated with causal bias. Prediction error is useful for assessing nuisance-function estimation, but it should not be treated as a direct measure of the quality of the resulting causal estimator.
item.dc:creator: Cong Cao
